The word turnover captures one core idea: things cycling out and being replaced. Think of it like a wheel turning — something goes out, something new comes in. This core idea plays out in several different areas of life, and once you grasp it, all the meanings will make perfect sense.

This is the most common meaning you'll encounter in business and finance.

A company's turnover is the total amount of money it earns from selling its goods or services over a period of time — usually a year. It is not profit. It is the raw total that flows in from customers before any costs are subtracted.

"The supermarket chain reported a turnover of ₹500 crore last year."

This means the supermarket collected ₹500 crore from customers through sales. Whether they made a profit after paying for rent, staff, and supplies is a separate question.

Why is it called "turnover"? Because money keeps cycling — goods go out, money comes in, you buy more goods, sell them again. The stock turns over, and each cycle generates revenue. The total of all those cycles is your turnover.

Key distinction to remember:

  • Turnover = all the money coming in from sales (also called revenue or gross sales)
  • Profit = what's left after you subtract all your costs from the turnover

If a business has a high turnover but high costs, it can still make very little profit — or even a loss.
2. In Employment: Staff or Employee Turnover

Employee turnover refers to the rate at which workers leave a company and are replaced by new ones.

"The restaurant has a very high turnover — most waiters quit within three months."

Again, the core idea of cycling applies: employees come in, leave, and new ones take their place. When this happens frequently, we say turnover is high. When employees stay for a long time, turnover is low.

High turnover is generally seen as a problem for companies. It costs money and time to hire and train new people repeatedly. It also signals that something may be wrong — poor management, low pay, bad working conditions, or a stressful environment.

Low turnover usually means employees are satisfied and choose to stay.

You'll often see phrases like:

"The tech startup struggled with high turnover."
"The school's low staff turnover meant students had consistent teachers for years."

This meaning is closely related to the business meaning above, but it focuses on physical goods rather than money.

Stock (or inventory) turnover refers to how quickly a business sells and replenishes its products.

"The electronics store has a high turnover on smartphones — they sell out every model within weeks."

If a shop buys 100 units of a product and sells all 100 quickly before restocking, that product has a high turnover. If items sit on shelves for months, turnover is low.

A high stock turnover is generally good — it means products are selling fast and cash isn't stuck in unsold goods. A low turnover can mean the business has bought too much stock, the products aren't popular, or they're priced too high.

In many team sports — especially basketball and American football — a turnover means a moment when one team unintentionally loses the ball to the opposing team, without the period of play ending naturally.

"The team committed five turnovers in the second half and lost the game."

A turnover happens through:

  • A fumble (dropping the ball, in American football)
  • An interception (the other team catches a pass meant for your teammate)
  • Stepping out of bounds while holding the ball
  • Violating a rule that gives the other team possession

The idea is the same: control of the ball turns over from one team to the other, unexpectedly. Turnovers are costly because they give the opponent an opportunity to score.
5. In Food: A Type of Pastry

A turnover is a small, individual pastry made by placing a filling on one half of a flat piece of dough, then folding (turning over) the other half on top of it, sealing the edges, and baking or frying it.

"She had an apple turnover with her morning tea."

Common fillings include apple, cherry, cheese, or chocolate. The pastry is typically triangular or semicircular in shape.

The name is very literal: the dough is turned over onto the filling.
6. The General Sense: Rate of Replacement

Outside of these specific contexts, turnover can describe how quickly anything is replaced or cycled through in a general sense.

"There's a fast turnover of customers at this café — people come in, order quickly, and leave."
"The turnover of fashion trends has gotten faster with social media."

Wherever something moves through a cycle — in and out, in and out — you can describe the speed of that cycle as its turnover.

The thread connecting every meaning is the same simple image: something cycling, replacing, or flipping over. Once that clicks, you'll recognize the word instantly in any context.
